changes.value: Crossan’s courtroom metaphor could become a transparent evidential model: classify each major claim by whether it appears in Mark, is copied or altered by Matthew and Luke, belongs to an independent tradition, or reflects later editorial development. Then give copied agreement no additional corroborative weight, while treating John’s possible knowledge of the Synoptics as a debated dependency rather than a certainty. The resulting map would show which claims remain independently supported after four apparent witnesses are reduced to distinguishable tradition streams.

A disciplined nonliteral reading needs a criterion for identifying when theological meaning survives historical doubt. Crossan could require the proposed meaning to arise from the narrative’s sequence and emphases: existing food passes through Jesus and reluctant disciples before becoming sufficient, while the Emmaus stranger is recognized through Scripture and shared hospitality. The criterion should also test rival readings, including White’s heavenly-bread discourse and prophetic-fulfillment emphasis, and concede uncertainty where those textual features support significance without determining whether the narrated event occurred.
